text.tspan: Spec Input System: Research Mind Map
Six interviews (P1 to P6), 30 cited excerpts, four pain clusters, twelve actions and five counter-evidence cards. Every action acts before code is generated.
P1 Senior full-stack engineer
P2 Senior / lead engineer · P3 Principal backend engineer · P4 Junior engineer, 10 months
P5 Director, Software Engineering, leads 12 engineers · P6 Senior full-stack engineer, new greenfield application
= new or changed in this version.
Orange text
(by participants): STRONG = 4 or more of 6 (solid fill) · MODERATE = 3 (solid outline) · LIMITED = 1 to 2 (dashed outline)
: FRONTSTAGE = what the engineer sees and does · BACKSTAGE = systems and processes behind it
Each action cites excerpt numbers from its own pain box.
Evidence strength
Cluster tag
As a Senior Software Engineer I want the system to detect
and surface architectural and query's missing context
gaps before code generation so that I can prevent
unauthorized agent inferences.
P6's “spec” is a plain-English prompt sent in small chunks,
with the chat history carrying the context. Actions here
apply to specs, prompts and chat sessions alike.
HOW MIGHT WE
automatically detect and surface
architectural and query missing context
gaps before code is generated to prevent
unauthorized agent inferences?
1. Context &
Dependency Gaps
P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6
EVIDENCE 6 of 6
BACKSTAGE
Pains & Evidence
Actions & Ideas
5. P4-Q: 'Where do you struggle most with controlling the AI's output?'
insight: Context is split across separate repositories and cannot go into one prompt [Interview P4, Q: Context Struggle]
6. P5-Q: 'Which details are most often missing from a spec?'
insight: Failure and negative scenarios; specs cover the happy path [Interview P5, Q: Missing Details]
7. P6-Q: 'When does a spec not work well?'
insight: Undocumented knowledge (URLs, how auth works) is invisible to the agent; “the hard part of the job is getting that information”
[Interview P6, Q: Spec Limits]
8. P6-Q: 'Tell me about a time the agent's output did not match your spec.'
insight: A debugging loop blamed the wrong cause because a file he had changed was never attached as context [Interview P6, Q: Output
Mismatch]
INTERVIEW EXCERPTS:
1. P1-Q: 'Do you face communication gaps?'
insight: PM acceptance criteria have gaps on edge cases [Interview P1, Q: Comm Gaps]
2. P1-Q: 'How often do hallucinations occur?'
insight: Hallucinations spike when larger context is missing [Interview P1, Q: Hallucinations]
3. P2-Q: 'What is the main failure mode?'
insight: Agent decides in the gap between spec and assumptions [Interview P2, Q: Failure Modes]
4. P3-Q: 'What details do you prompt?'
insight: Needs verbose domain & tech stack context to prevent errors [Interview P3, Q: Prompting Details]
• Context sits in other repos or undocumented sources the agent cannot see
• Incomplete specs written by non-engineers omit edge cases & rules
• Causes agent hallucinations & unauthorized inferences
PAIN POINTS:
Automated Pre-Ingestion Context Compiler
STRONG · P1 P3 P4 P6
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
. Also suggests which files and repositories to attach, so the context is neither missing
nor wasteful.
A tool that automatically gathers and compiles all necessary project context (codebase structure, domain
rules, project history) before handing off a specification to an AI agent. Instead of relying on a developer to
manually upload or explain background context every time, the compiler prepares a complete context
package automatically
The engineer sends a complete, right-sized context package without hunting for files.
excerpts 2, 4, 5, 8 · P1 P3 P4 P6
Cross-check specs against repo patterns & vector
knowledge bases
MODERATE · P1 P2 P3
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
Automatically scanning written specifications against existing code repositories, design patterns, and
company knowledge bases. This ensures the AI uses established code patterns and project structures rather
than inventing its own incompatible patterns
Generated code fits existing repo patterns instead of inventing incompatible ones.
excerpts 2, 3, 4 · P1 P2 P3
Surface missing API/data dependencies prior to agent
execution
MODERATE · P1 P5 P6
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
. Also flags undefined failure
paths (error codes, no-access cases) and undocumented facts such as URLs and auth flows, with who owns
them.
Scanning the written feature request to spot missing backend APIs, database schemas, or external
dependencies before the AI starts generating code. If a required API endpoint or database field isn't defined,
the system alerts the team upfront so developers don't face broken code late
Gaps are raised before generation, not found in review or testing.
excerpts 1, 6, 7 · P1 P5 P6
2. Architectural
Guardrails & System
P1 P2 P3 P5 P6
EVIDENCE 5 of 6
BACKSTAGE
Pains & Evidence
Actions & Ideas
5. P5-Q: 'How different is spec-driven development from vibe coding?'
insight: A spec works like bowling bumpers: guardrails the LLM works inside [Interview P5, Q: SDD vs Vibe Coding]
6. P5-Q: 'How do you review AI-generated code, and how do you know it followed the spec?'
insight: Tests cover function; coding standards rely on engineers and defined .md files [Interview P5, Q: Review Method]
7. P6-Q: 'If you could change one thing about how you give specs to the AI?'
insight: Agent puts types and constants in one file, against the team's folder structure; he wants it aligned to his coding standards
[Interview P6, Q: Wish Change]
INTERVIEW EXCERPTS:
1. P1-Q: 'How do you check code against rules?'
insight: AI uses unapproved libraries outside company standards [Interview P1, Q: Rule Check]
2. P2-Q: 'What structural inconsistencies occur?'
insight: Agent misses existing utilities and reinvents algorithms [Interview P2, Q: Code Structure]
3. P1-Q: 'What is your primary concern?'
insight: AI code runs technically but fails scalability & design rules [Interview P1, Q: Primary Concern]
4. P3-Q: 'How does AI choose paths?'
insight: AI picks unoptimized roads leading to downstream tech debt [Interview P3, Q: AI Path Choice]
• Agents introduce unapproved libraries & frameworks
• Reinventing existing utility functions from scratch
• Non-scalable code & technical debt creation
• Generated code ignores the team's style and file structure
PAIN POINTS:
Static Spec Validator checking specs against corporate tech
stack rules
MODERATE · P1 P5 P6
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
Also reads the team's instruction files (.md) and checks naming, file structure, and where shared code, types
and constants belong.
A software rule-checker that evaluates the prompt or feature spec against company tech stack standards
(e.g., allowed languages, frameworks, or libraries) before code generation. This prevents the AI from
introducing unapproved third-party packages or using forbidden frameworks.
Output follows the team's standards; P6 expects this would make his job “10% easier.”
excerpts 1, 3, 6, 7 · P1 P5 P6
Automated design system component matching
LIMITED · P2 only
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
Kept, but flagged: P5 and P6 did not mention it. Revisit in the next round.
A tool that inspects UI mockups and specifications, automatically linking proposed visual elements to pre-built
company design system components. This prevents AI agents from re-creating custom UI components from
scratch when reusable components already exist in the repository.
Reusable UI components are reused, not rebuilt.
excerpt 2 · P2 only
Pre-flight security & architecture guardrail verification
MODERATE · P1 P3 P5
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
An automated check performed prior to execution that evaluates architectural and security constraints—such
as data privacy policies, cloud infrastructure spending limits, and authentication rules. It flags high-risk
actions (like spinning up costly server instances or bypassing security checks) before the AI can execute
them.
High-risk actions (cost, security, production data) are caught before the agent can run
them.
excerpts 3, 4, 5 · P1 P3 P5
3. Cross-Functional
Handoff & Alignment
P1 P2 P4 P5 P6
EVIDENCE 5 of 6
FRONTSTAGE
Pains & Evidence
Actions & Ideas
INTERVIEW EXCERPTS:
1. P2-Q: 'What is missing from UX mockups?'
insight: Static comps show look but omit 76 conditional states [Interview P2, Q: UX Mockups]
2. P1-Q: 'Where do specification gaps originate?'
insight: PM acceptance criteria lack technical depth on edge cases [Interview P1, Q: Spec Origins]
3. P1-Q: 'Where is communication breakdown?'
insight: Disparate mental models cause UI and backend data state drift [Interview P1, Q: Breakdown]
4. P4-Q: 'What is classic handoff problem?'
insight: Static design handoff results in visual & logical divergence [Interview P4, Q: Handoff Problem]
5. P5-Q: 'How do you hand specifications to your engineers?'
insight: No specific process; the product owner sets backlog priority and engineers pick up work as they have time [Interview P5, Q:
Handoff Process]
6. P5-Q: 'When an agent hits something the spec did not cover, what happens?'
insight: The engineer decides, or takes it back to the product owner to define the expected behavior [Interview P5, Q: Uncovered Gaps]
7. P6-Q: 'How do you turn the product owner's acceptance criteria into what you give an agent?'
insight: Criteria are end-user focused, not tied to the codebase architecture, so he adds direction and splits the work into sequential
chunks [Interview P6, Q: Criteria to Prompt]
• Misalignment between static visual mockups & 76+ interactive states
• PM acceptance criteria lack technical depth
• Breakdown between design intent and developer implementation
PAIN POINTS:
Pre-Spec Handoff Analyzer
LIMITED · P1 P6
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
Also lists what end-user acceptance criteria leave out, such as architecture direction, which engineers like P6
add by hand.
A digital collaboration tool used when transitioning work from UX Design and Product Management to
Engineering. It analyzes design files and acceptance criteria to ensure technical constraints and user flows
are aligned across teams before engineering begins.
Acceptance criteria reach the engineer with technical direction attached.
excerpts 2, 3, 7 · P1 P6
Highlight missing interactive states & UI/backend data
discrepancies
MODERATE · P1 P2 P4
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
An automated audit that flags unhandled UI states (e.g., hover states, loading screens, error messages, or
complex conditional views) and discrepancies between frontend visual screens and backend data structures.
For instance, if a design comp shows 2 states but an object has 76 conditional backend states, the system
surfaces those unmapped states upfront.
Missing states are found before the build, not in review.
excerpts 1, 3, 4 · P1 P2 P4
Shared multi-disciplinary specification review checkpoint
LIMITED · P5 only · REFRAMED
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
Reframed after P5: no formal handoff exists today, so route each gap question to the product owner or tech
lead and record the answer, instead of adding a sign-off meeting.
A formal, collaborative review step where Designers, Product Managers, and Engineers review and sign off on
the specification together before passing it to AI agents. This guarantees that all three roles share a single
mental model and agree on exact feature behavior.
Gap questions reach the owner who can answer them, and the answer is recorded.
excerpts 5, 6 · P5 only
4. Intent Verification &
Decision Traceability
P1 P2 P4 P5 P6
EVIDENCE 5 of 6
FRONTSTAGE + BACKSTAGE
Pains & Evidence
Actions & Ideas
INTERVIEW EXCERPTS:
1. P2-Q: 'Where does AI context live?'
insight: Context trapped in isolated continuous chat sessions teammates can't see [Interview P2, Q: Context Location]
2. P2-Q: 'How deep are code reviews?'
insight: Human review depth dropped to skimming while code volume surged [Interview P2, Q: Review Depth]
3. P1-Q: 'What is missing from AI outputs?'
insight: AI fails to explain 'why' it chose a path or alternative trade-offs [Interview P1, Q: AI Output Gaps]
4. P4-Q: 'Why is traceability critical?'
insight: Debugging agent errors requires hunting unrecorded assumption phases [Interview P4, Q: Traceability Needs]
5. P5-Q: 'When would you want to see what the AI assumed: before, during or after code?'
insight: Before code: cheaper in tokens and time; plan first, execute once the plan is right [Interview P5, Q: Timing]
6. P5-Q: 'If you could change one thing about how specs are given to the AI?'
insight: Trust comes when the LLM asks intuitive questions about gaps and rationale, not just “is it okay to do this?” [Interview P5, Q: Wish
Change]
7. P6-Q: 'When an agent reaches something the spec did not cover, does it ask or assume?'
insight: “Most of the time, it just assumes” [Interview P6, Q: Ask or Assume]
8. P6-Q: 'At what point would you want the agent to stop and ask?'
insight: Questions are missing before and during code; he sometimes has to prompt it to “let me know” when unsure [Interview P6, Q: Stop
and Ask]
• Context & decisions trapped in unshared developer chat sessions
• Skimming code reviews due to high AI code volume
• AI agents lack 'why' explanations for architectural choices
PAIN POINTS:
Shared Spec Audit Log & Decision Traceability Layer
MODERATE · P1 P2 P4
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
A centralized history log that records prompt exchanges, context additions, and architectural decisions made
during AI interactions. Instead of context being lost in isolated developer chat sessions, the entire team has
visibility into why certain decisions were made.
A teammate can see why a decision was made without asking the original engineer.
excerpts 1, 3, 4 · P1 P2 P4
Record AI assumptions and force explicit human gating
STRONG · P2 P4 P5 P6
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
Shows the assumptions as a plan before code is written, since P5 wants to review the plan first.
System checkpoints that capture any assumptions the AI agent makes when facing ambiguous requirements
and require a human engineer or designer to explicitly review and approve them before proceeding. This
prevents the agent from making unauthorized inferences or choices silently.
Engineers approve or correct each assumption before code exists, saving tokens and
rework.
excerpts 2, 4, 5, 7 · P2 P4 P5 P6
Ask-before-assume prompts at spec gaps
LIMITED · P5 P6 · NEW
OPPORTUNITY →
EVIDENCE →
When the agent reaches something the spec does not cover, it asks a specific question instead of assuming.
Questions appear before and during generation, and only for gaps that matter, so engineers are not flooded
with prompts.
The agent stops at real gaps without being told to “let me know” each time.
excerpts 6, 7, 8 · P5 P6
WHY PARKED →
A visual interface that maps each generated code block directly back to its corresponding specification requirement or acceptance criterion, while highlighting high-risk code
changes for deeper human review. This allows reviewers to focus their attention on critical logic rather than skimming massive volumes of generated code.
It works after code exists, and the HMW is scoped to before code is generated. Linked evidence: branch 4, excerpt 2 (P2: reviews dropped to skimming). Revisit
if the scope widens.
PARKED · FROM BRANCH 4 · IDEA C: Surface risk alerts and requirement-to-code mapping
COUNTER-EVIDENCE: where the interviews disagree with the map
Kept visible so the four clusters are not read as unanimous. Each card says what it challenges and how the map responds.
CHALLENGES →
MAP RESPONDS →
On writing a detailed spec up front: it “doesn't lead to more correct code or more like productivity gains.”
That engineers write a full spec before the AI builds. P6 sends plain-English prompts in
small chunks and corrects as he goes.
Actions apply to specs, prompts and chat sessions alike. The scope note under the
root says so.
P6 · CHALLENGES THE PREMISE
CHALLENGES →
MAP RESPONDS →
“I've never felt that spec-driven development is realistic.” He adds that it is more realistic now that LLMs
do the implementation.
That spec-driven development is mainstream practice.
Claims are scoped to teams that choose it. P6 sees it as most useful for “multi-file,
multi class features.”
P5 · CHALLENGES THE PREMISE
CHALLENGES →
MAP RESPONDS →
On what is missing from AI explanations: “99% of the time. It's not lacking.” He says you can just ask the
AI questions.
P1's pain point that agents lack the “why.”
Kept as a split finding. The audit log records the “why,” so it does not depend on
remembering to ask.
P4 · CHALLENGES BRANCH 4
CHALLENGES →
MAP RESPONDS →
Asked for a time an AI made a choice nobody asked for: “I don't really have a good answer for that
question.” His agent use is focused, so there is less room to go haywire.
How often unauthorized inferences happen.
Frequency stays an open question for the research agenda. P6 reports the agent
“most of the time” assumes at a gap.
P5 · CHALLENGES BRANCHES 1 AND 4
CHALLENGES →
MAP RESPONDS →
When the agent goes off track: “most of the time it's user error.” The prompt was not specific enough.
Framing the problem as agent hallucination rather than an under-specified prompt.
The HMW detects the gap before generation, so it holds whether the gap came from
the engineer or the agent.
P6 · CHALLENGES BRANCH 1
each action cites excerpt numbers from its own pain box · each excerpt cites the interview and question · evidence strength counts distinct participants · sources are Interviews P1 to P6.
